newsitem.title: USA: Dow seen opening lower, more selling expected.
newsitem.headline: Dow seen opening lower, more selling expected.

text.p: U.S. stocks should open lower Friday following heavy selling late yesterday that sent the Dow to a loss of nearly 100 points on the busiest trading day ever.
The Dow closed off 94 points at 6756.
The losses, sparked by higher interest rates and negative technical indicators in the futures market, wiped out the Dow's first foray above 6900 and sheared 1.4 percent off the blue-chip index.
The Dow closed 150 points below its high for the day.
"We should open down about 20 points or so," judging from the Standard & Poor's March futures contract, said Prudential Securities analyst Larry Wachtel.
He expects further declines but then stabilization: "You can't stop a powerful market on a random Thursday. The market may top out but it takes time."
He added, "Let's face it -- the Dow was up 400 points in three weeks and IBM is up 70 points since July. The index was very vulnerable. We were cruising for a bruising."
The Standard & Poor's March futures were off about three points to 777 ahead of the opening.
The long bond was off two ticks to yield 6.86 percent, with no major economic data due.
Global stocks sank in response to the Dow's pounding.
Hong Kong stocks fell sharply. The Hang Seng index lost 231 points, or 1.7 percent, to 13,379.
London's FTSE 100 Index was off one percent at the start of trading, opening down 41.5 points. At midday it was off 48 at 4223.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column says the stocks of small-cap firms bought by Jeffrey Vinik, former manager of Fidelity Investments's Magellan fund, have been surging.
The New York Times's Market Place column examines the notion that the outcome of the Super Bowl can predict the stock market's performance for the year.
